title: 2037625 Ontario Inc. / ITC Invoice to Cash (2015 TCC)
subject: Software company SR&ED appeal regarding invoice-to-cash financial software development and technological uncertainty.
summary: In 2037625 Ontario Inc. (formerly ITC Invoice to Cash Inc.) v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 269, the Tax Court of Canada upheld the denial of an Ontario factoring company's $32,425 SR&ED investment tax credit claim for Factorsuite software integration. For Canadian software claimants, the key takeaway is that interfacing systems using standard programming techniques involves no technological uncertainty.
metaDescription: Learn about the October 2015 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED ruling for 2037625 Ontario Inc. (formerly ITC Invoice to Cash Inc.).

body.text: Section 1: Executive Summary and Case Background
Overview of the Litigation and Corporate Context

On October 30, 2015, the Tax Court of Canada rendered its decision in 2037625 Ontario Inc. (formerly ITC Invoice to Cash Inc.) v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2015 TCC 269, which is correspondingly indexed in French Canadian jurisprudence as 2015 CCI 269. The appeal arose from a Notice of Reassessment for the appellant's 2008 taxation year (ending August 31, 2008), issued by the Minister of National Revenue (the Minister), administered through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which reduced to nil the appellant's claim for Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) of $32,425 arising from its claim for allowable Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) expenditures of $69,354 under the federal Income Tax Act (the Act); although the amount in dispute exceeded $25,000, the appellant elected to proceed under the Informal Procedure and to limit the amount in appeal to $25,000 (2015 TCC 269, paras. 1–2).

Prior to its corporate name change to 2037625 Ontario Inc., the appellant operated commercially as ITC Invoice to Cash Inc., a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) incorporated in December 2003 with its head office in Mississauga, Ontario, which offered financial “factoring” services to its business clients—purchasing their accounts receivable at a discount, advancing 90 percent of the invoice amount and withholding the remaining 10 percent as a fee deposit (2015 TCC 269, para. 3). In the course of developing its own Factorsuite software package—a web-based, integrated account management solution for factoring companies and their business clients, referred to as the Factorsuite Optimization Project—the appellant claimed SR&ED expenditures of $69,354 and corresponding ITCs of $32,425 for its software development activities (2015 TCC 269, paras. 1 and 4). The disputed technical activities centred on three objectives: interfacing Factorsuite with the third-party factoring software Factorsoft and its predecessor FactorPC (owned by Bayside, which refused to share the internal code of its proprietary software) while maintaining the integrity of their calculations; integrating Factorsuite with the ActFax faxing software so that unique, personalized client reports could be faxed in the correct order and in real time; and achieving “interoperability and scalability” so that balances, statements of account and historical transaction data could be presented to clients instantaneously, including by reducing caching time and speeding up report generation (2015 TCC 269, paras. 6–10 and 23).
The Taxpayer's Claim and the Minister's Challenge

The appellant contended that its software development and system integration efforts constituted eligible "experimental development" pursuant to paragraph (c) of the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Act. The taxpayer's legal and technical position rested on the premise that its technological uncertainties arose from the lack of information about the proprietary third-party products—information unavailable even from the software supplier—and that it had resolved them through systematic experimentation using data mining and data mapping and, according to its expert witness Victor Sarmiento, “process mining” (a discipline he testified was only named after an Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers task force was established in 2009), formulating hypotheses, pursuing five or six different approaches to reducing caching time, and conducting hypothetical transactions in a scientifically designed test environment (2015 TCC 269, paras. 11–13, 24 and 29).

The Minister challenged the claim at both the technical and evidentiary levels, maintaining that the disputed activities did not satisfy the statutory definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the Act. Specifically, the CRA's reviewer, Leon Pellissero, testified that the techniques used—data mining, data mapping, process mining and caching—were routine procedures that any competent computer programmer using industry standard methods would utilize, and that, although the structures of the third-party products were unknown, the main challenge of obtaining information from one product and moving it to another could be resolved by well-known techniques rather than requiring a systematic investigation aimed at resolving genuine technological uncertainty (2015 TCC 269, paras. 16 and 27–28). Because the underlying methods used to achieve the software interfacing were known and available within the common stock of software engineering knowledge—Mr. Pellissero testified that the process mining technique existed in 2007 and that information on it was available—the Minister asserted that no scientific or technological risk existed (2015 TCC 269, paras. 17 and 30).
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

Within the Canadian federal tax system, the SR&ED program operates through a bifurcated statutory mechanism under the Income Tax Act. First, subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct qualifying current and capital SR&ED expenditures via an indefinite expenditure pool (capital expenditures were ineligible for property acquired after 2013 and before December 16, 2024), while subsection 127(5) provides for the deduction of ITCs calculated on qualified expenditures as defined in subsection 127(9)—at a general rate of 15% (20% for taxation years before 2014, including the appellant's 2008 taxation year) or an enhanced 35% rate for qualifying CCPCs, with refundability governed by section 127.1—with unused credits subject to a 20-year carryforward period. Second, the statutory gateway to both the subsection 37(1) expenditure deduction and the subsection 127(5) ITC is the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Act, which consolidated statutory language formerly housed in subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations.

Under subsection 248(1) of the Act, SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and encompasses three foundational categories of eligible core work. Paragraph 248(1)(a) covers basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(b) encompasses applied research, which is work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Most relevant to commercial software claimants, paragraph 248(1)(c) governs experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Furthermore, paragraph 248(1)(d) permits commensurate support work—such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—only where the taxpayer first establishes that an eligible core project under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) exists. Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude routine data collection, market research, quality control, routine testing, style changes, and commercial production from SR&ED eligibility.

To operationalize subsection 248(1), the Tax Court of Canada in 2037625 Ontario Inc. applied the seminal five-question judicial framework established by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), whose criteria were confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, 99 DTC 5087, and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, and which forms the legal foundation of the CRA's administrative two-step methodology in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (2015 TCC 269, para. 19). Under this binding jurisprudential standard, a claimant must prove on a balance of probabilities that five cumulative conditions were met. First, there must have been a scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be removed by standard practice, routine engineering, or habitual procedures. Second, the effort must have involved formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the overall approach adopted must have comported with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through experiment or analysis. Fourth, the process must have resulted in a technological advancement, representing an increase in the stock of technological knowledge even if the functional attempt ultimately failed. Fifth, a detailed contemporaneous record of the hypotheses tested and the results achieved must have been maintained as the work progressed.
The Court's Final Holding

The Tax Court of Canada dismissed the appeal of 2037625 Ontario Inc., upholding the Minister's denial of the SR&ED claim in its entirety. Applying Judge Bowman's criteria in Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Diane Campbell held that the appellant had not met its onus on a balance of probabilities because the evidence did not demonstrate that its activities were anything more than routine engineering or standard procedures, and she preferred the evidence of the Respondent's witness, Mr. Pellissero—whom she did not accept as an expert—over that of the appellant's qualified expert, Mr. Sarmiento, because it was presented with greater clarity and was, in the end, more convincing (2015 TCC 269, paras. 21–22). Because the appellant utilized well-known, standard programming procedures—data mining, data mapping, process mining, caching and a routine fax-ordering procedure—to interface its Factorsuite software with the third-party Factorsoft, FactorPC and ActFax applications, the Court held that no scientific or technological uncertainty existed under paragraph 248(1)(c) of the Act (2015 TCC 269, paras. 30–32). The Court further and independently found that the appellant had demonstrated only a product improvement and an advancement for the company rather than an advancement in the underlying technology, and that it had not shown that hypotheses were specifically formulated and tested in accordance with the scientific method or that a detailed record was kept as the work progressed; consequently, the claimed expenditures were not qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9) and the ITCs were properly disallowed (2015 TCC 269, paras. 36–41).
Section 2: Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
Conflation of Functional Product Novelty with Technological Uncertainty

The primary legal deficiency that proved fatal to the appellant's case in 2037625 Ontario Inc. was the fundamental conflation of commercial or functional product development with technological uncertainty. In software engineering claims, taxpayers frequently equate the difficulty of building a complex, integrated business application—such as an automated invoice-to-cash factoring platform—with experimental development. However, Canadian tax jurisprudence draws an uncompromising boundary between technical problems, which are resolved by applying known coding architectures, vendor documentation, and professional skill, and technological uncertainty, which arises only when the capability or method to achieve an objective cannot be determined or predicted based on publicly available scientific or technological knowledge and standard practice.

In Paragraph 35 of the judgment, after likening the case to Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65 (in which a “crawler” technique was held to be standard practice), the Court addressed the analogy that the appellant's own expert, Mr. Sarmiento, had drawn between the use of log files in computer programming and microscopes in cancer research, explaining why achieving a new outcome through standard techniques fails paragraph 248(1)(c) of the Act (2015 TCC 269, paras. 14 and 35). The Court observed that the SR&ED regime demands substantially more than merely conducting standard observations or applying known tools, stating expressly that “the SR&ED regime requires more than just looking into a microscope for research” (« Le régime de RS-DE exige davantage que simplement regarder dans un microscope pour faire de la recherche »). Responding to Mr. Sarmiento's example of looking at cancer cells, the Court explained that eligible SR&ED would require the addition of a new substance into cancer cells under a microscope, the removal of a specific component, or the amalgam of two different techniques to create something new. The Court stated that such methods fall within the ambit of technological advancement.

Conversely, the Court emphasized that if a new product or functional outcome is created using well-known, standard techniques, it cannot be classified as an SR&ED activity because standard techniques do not involve scientific or technological risk or uncertainty. Even if a project leads to significant practical progress in a field, there is no scientific or technological uncertainty within the meaning of Northwest Hydraulic if standard practice is employed. As the Court noted, a scientist attempting to cure cancer by doing nothing other than observing cancer cell interactions under a microscope would not meet the requirements of SR&ED under paragraph 248(1)(c) of the Act, because the element of uncertainty was eliminated by using solely standard, well-known observational practices. Applied directly to the appellant's software projects, the Court found that the techniques used to determine what data was contained in the unknown third-party programs and how it could interact with Factorsuite, the procedure and holding area used to send faxes in the correct order, and the procedures used to process, cache and refresh client reports were all available standard procedures routinely used by competent programmers—even though Bayside had refused to share the internal code of its software (2015 TCC 269, paras. 10 and 30–32). The fact that the third-party products belonging to Bayside and ActFax were unknown to the appellant was an additional challenge, but the Court held that it could not by itself constitute a technological uncertainty, and that the interoperability or scalability of unknown programs could not be the technological advancement because a vast number of programs interact with each other every day (2015 TCC 269, para. 37).
Absence of a Structured Process of Hypothesis-Driven Experimentation

In addition to, and independently of, the appellant's reliance on standard software engineering procedures, the Court found a failure to demonstrate a systematic investigation carried out by means of experiment or analysis, as mandated by the preamble to subsection 248(1) and the second and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic (2015 TCC 269, para. 40). In software integration projects, developers routinely encounter software bugs, data-mapping mismatches, API payload discrepancies, and user interface adjustments. Resolving such obstacles via trial-and-error debugging—where a programmer writes integration code, observes an error message, consults third-party commercial software documentation, and modifies the syntax—does not constitute the scientific method.

In 2037625 Ontario Inc., although both Mr. Caicedo and Mr. Sarmiento testified that the appellant undertook multiple hypotheses to make the differing programs interoperable—for example, whether a plain text file containing all of the required information could be created to resolve the faxing problem—the Court held that none of those hypotheses was reflective of the scientific research method, and it was given no evidence of the number of tests performed, the nature of the experiments, the modifications made or the results obtained (2015 TCC 269, para. 40). Having found no technological uncertainty, the Court characterized the work as nothing more than routine engineering or standard procedures, which, under the first criterion articulated by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic, cannot give rise to technological uncertainty within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the Act (2015 TCC 269, paras. 20–21).
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation of Technological Obstacles

Under the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic—which the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, at paragraph 17, described as requiring that a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results achieved be kept as the work progressed—a claimant, who bears the onus of proof on a balance of probabilities, is expected to produce contemporaneous records generated as the work progressed that document the specific hypotheses formulated, the experimental architectures tested, and the analytical conclusions reached (2015 TCC 269, paras. 19, 21 and 40). While the Tax Court of Canada recognizes that the absence of formal academic laboratory notebooks is not automatically fatal if convincing oral and documentary evidence proves the scientific method was followed, general business records—such as commercial project plans, user interface wireframes, invoice logs, or high-level functional release notes—cannot substitute for technical evidence of experimentation.

In 2037625 Ontario Inc., the evidentiary record placed before the Tax Court judge demonstrated a product improvement that benefitted the company—namely, the integration of the Factorsuite, Factorsoft, FactorPC and ActFax programs—rather than what technological limitations were systematically investigated; very little supporting documentation of testing was introduced, some of it consisted of handwritten notes not in English for which no translation was provided, and no reasonable explanation was offered for the failure to keep a detailed record (2015 TCC 269, paras. 36 and 40). Notably, in a decision by the same judge, Justice Diane Campbell, released just three days earlier (on October 27, 2015)—ACSIS EHR (Electronic Health Record) Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 263—the Tax Court reached the opposite conclusion and allowed, with costs, an SR&ED claim for the development of a multi-write database replication system supporting a nation-wide health information system in Belize's unreliable network environment, because credible and largely unchallenged oral testimony, together with contemporaneous notes and whiteboard photos, established technological uncertainties that could not be resolved through routine engineering or standard procedures and a systematic investigation to resolve them, even though the Court found the documentation less detailed than it would have liked. By contrast, cases from the same period such as R&D PRO-innovation Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 186—where the Court accepted that the testing was methodical and systematic but dismissed the appeal because no technological uncertainty beyond standard procedures and routine engineering was shown—and Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313—where the Court ruled in the taxpayer's favour and indicated that contemporaneous documentation, though recommended, is not essential—illustrate that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria are applied to the totality of the evidence rather than as a rigid documentary test. The divergence between 2037625 Ontario Inc. (2015 TCC 269) and ACSIS EHR (2015 TCC 263) underscores that software development involving the exchange of data between systems is not per se ineligible in Canada, but fails whenever the taxpayer's documentary and oral evidence describes functional integration achieved through standard procedures rather than a systematic investigation of technological uncertainty that routine engineering could not resolve.
Third-Party Commercial Software and Expenditure Eligibility Deficiencies

Beyond the core scientific eligibility failure under subsection 248(1), the ruling did not separately analyze the characterization of third-party commercial software costs or third-party expenditures under section 37 of the Act; having found that the work was not SR&ED, the Court held only that the claimed expenditures were not qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9), so the following considerations reflect general statutory context rather than holdings of the Court (2015 TCC 269, para. 41). Where a claimant purchases or licenses third-party commercial software to incorporate into a larger experimental software application, the mere configuration, parameterization, or standard API linking of that purchased software does not transform the commercial software or the integration labour into SR&ED. Moreover, statutory amendments to section 37 and subsection 127(9), applicable to expenditures made after 2013 (and therefore not to the appellant's 2008 taxation year), eliminated capital expenditures (including capitalizable commercial software licences and capital assets) from SR&ED eligibility, restricting material expenditures strictly to materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED. The Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3; Bill C-15, assented to March 26, 2026) restored the eligibility of capital expenditures for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024.

Furthermore, claimants must strictly distinguish between expenditures for SR&ED performed directly on behalf of the taxpayer by arm's-length contractors under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)—where the taxpayer directs the technical experimentation and bears the technological risk—and third-party payments under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii), or ordinary commercial vendor service fees for implementing third-party software. Similarly, user interface development is eligible as commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) only to the strict extent that a rudimentary interface is required to test an underlying experimental hypothesis, whereas commercial user interface development is ineligible. Where external vendors or internal engineering teams merely execute functional tasks to deploy commercial software without contractual and operational governance isolating experimental tasks, the entire expenditure stream is disqualified.
Section 3: Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in 2037625 Ontario Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 269, against the taxpayer's specific legal and evidentiary failures and the governing standard of proof required by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in 2037625 Ontario Inc. (2015 TCC 269)
Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Threshold

cells: 1. Existence of Scientific or Technological Uncertainty
Paragraph 248(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act; Northwest Hydraulic (98 DTC 1839, Criterion 1).

Framed the functional challenge of interfacing its proprietary Factorsuite software with the third-party Factorsoft, FactorPC and ActFax software as an uncertainty, despite relying on known, standard programming techniques (data mining, data mapping, process mining and caching).

The claimant must prove on a balance of probabilities that a system-level constraint or technological limitation existed that could not be resolved by standard practice, routine engineering, or vendor documentation.
2. Formulation of Technological Hypotheses
Preamble to subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act; Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2).

Although its witnesses testified to multiple hypotheses aimed at making the programs interoperable (e.g., whether a plain text file could be created to resolve the faxing problem), none of the hypotheses aimed at the alleged uncertainties was reflective of the scientific research method.
Must articulate explicit, falsifiable hypotheses proposing how and why a novel algorithmic, architectural, or scientific mechanism will resolve the identified technological uncertainty.
3. Systematic Investigation by Experiment or Analysis
Preamble to subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act; Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 3).

Engaged in data mining, data mapping, log-file analysis (“process mining”), caching and routine report and fax-ordering procedures that the Court held were standard procedures (“just looking into a microscope for research” / applying well-known techniques), and produced no evidence of the number of tests, the nature of the experiments, the modifications or the results.

Must demonstrate strict adherence to the scientific method: defining control metrics, executing structured experimental protocols, measuring quantitative performance data, and iteratively modifying the hypothesis.
4. Achievement of Technological Advancement
Paragraph 248(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act; Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4).
Conflated the creation of a new commercial software feature or interfaced application with an advancement in underlying computer science or software engineering technology.
Must prove that the investigation generated new technological knowledge that advances the baseline of a competent professional in the field (even if the commercial product ultimately fails).
5. Contemporaneous Technical Documentation
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5); C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, para. 17.

Introduced very little supporting documentation of its testing—some of it handwritten notes not in English with no translation—and offered no reasonable explanation for its failure to keep a detailed record of hypotheses, tests and results as the work progressed.

Northwest Hydraulic expects a detailed record kept as the work progresses; although the Act contains no legislative requirement to produce such documents and credible oral testimony may suffice (ACSIS EHR, 2015 TCC 263, para. 39), dated technical artifacts generated during the taxation year (architecture logs, benchmark test matrices, commit histories tied to hypotheses) remain the most persuasive verification of the experimental progression.
6. Third-Party Software & Support Work Segregation
Paragraph 248(1)(d) & Subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act.

Not examined by the Court: because no eligible paragraph 248(1)(c) work was found, the Court did not reach the segregation of support work, user interface development or third-party software costs, and held only that the expenditures were not qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9).

Support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) (coding, testing, UI needed strictly for testing) is eligible only when directly commensurate with, and segregated from routine commercial work supporting, a valid paragraph 248(1)(c) project.

body.text: Section 4: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian corporate claimants and their tax advisors can proactively structure software and engineering initiatives to avoid the fatal pitfalls identified in 2037625 Ontario Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 269, the following two applied case studies examine high-risk industry scenarios and prescribe step-by-step legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary remediations.
Case Study 1: FinTech — Real-Time Factoring and Heterogeneous ERP Interfacing Architecture
Baseline Project Scenario and the "2037625 Ontario Inc." Pitfall

A Toronto-based CCPC, Apex Factoring Technologies Inc. (Apex), develops cloud-based supply-chain finance and automated invoice-discounting software. During its taxation year, Apex undertakes a major software initiative to interface its proprietary credit-scoring and ledger platform with three third-party commercial Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems used by its mid-market commercial clients. Left unstructured, Apex's engineering team characterizes the project on CRA Form T661 as developing a real-time bi-directional software interface to integrate Apex's proprietary invoice-to-cash engine with third-party commercial ERP systems and building a custom user dashboard. During a CRA technical and financial review, the Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) denies the claim in full, citing 2037625 Ontario Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 269. The RTA concludes that writing API connectors, parsing XML/JSON payloads, handling webhook retries, and building user interfaces involve standard, well-known software engineering techniques lacking any scientific or technological uncertainty.
Step 1: Project Governance and Boundary Segregation (Isolating the Experimental Kernel)

To satisfy paragraph 248(1)(c) and paragraph 248(1)(d) of the Act, Apex must restructure its internal project governance at project inception by separating the commercial integration project from the SR&ED experimental project. Apex's Chief Technology Officer (CTO) and SR&ED tax counsel establish an internal governance charter that explicitly excludes standard REST and SOAP API development, data-schema mapping, authentication handshakes, and commercial user interface development from the SR&ED claim pool. Instead, governance is narrowed strictly to an underlying system-level architecture conflict: when synchronizing high-velocity invoice state mutations across legacy, single-threaded third-party ERP databases and Apex's distributed, multi-tenant event-driven ledger under strict sub-50-millisecond latency constraints, standard distributed locking protocols (such as Two-Phase Commit or standard Saga patterns) induce lock contention and non-deterministic state divergence because the third-party commercial ERP engines do not expose transaction-log hooks. Consequently, the technological uncertainty is defined specifically as whether a lock-free, speculative state-reconciliation algorithm can guarantee ACID-equivalent serializability across opaque, black-box third-party database engines without access to internal write-ahead logs.
Step 2: Structuring the Process of Experimentation (Overcoming Paragraph 35 of 2037625 Ontario Inc.)

To avoid the Court's criticism in Paragraph 35 of 2037625 Ontario Inc.—that using known techniques to create a new product is akin to merely looking into a microscope—Apex institutes a formal hypothesis-and-experimentation protocol. Before writing any experimental code, the engineering team conducts and logs baseline tests using standard polling and webhook queuing techniques, proving quantitatively that standard procedures fail at concurrency loads exceeding 400 transactions per second (TPS) due to third-party ERP thread exhaustion. Once the failure of standard practice is empirically established, the engineers formulate specific, falsifiable hypotheses—such as hypothesizing that combining a Conflict-Free Replicated Data Type (CRDT) delta-state buffer with an adaptive predictive back-pressure controller will eliminate phantom invoice double-pledging while maintaining sub-50ms synchronization latency across non-cooperative third-party persistence layers. Each development sprint is then structured around a controlled experimental iteration in which specific algorithmic variables are modified, stress-tested against synthetic high-concurrency workloads, and analyzed for mathematical convergence and state consistency.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation Architecture

To satisfy the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic and survive Tax Court scrutiny, Apex configures its software development lifecycle (SDLC) tools to generate audit-ready contemporaneous evidence as the work progresses. Within its issue-tracking and version-control repositories, Apex creates a dedicated "SR&ED Technological Uncertainty" classification. Code commits and pull requests touching the experimental state-reconciliation kernel are linked directly to specific Hypothesis IDs rather than commercial feature tickets, cleanly segregating eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) programming from excluded commercial coding. Simultaneously, automated Continuous Integration (CI) pipelines archive time-stamped performance telemetry logs showing failed algorithmic iterations—such as memory leaks and state-divergence rates at 1,000 TPS—alongside engineering post-mortems explaining why an experimental architecture failed and how the hypothesis was reformulated.
Step 4: Contractual and Financial Tracking Restructuring

Where Apex engages external software specialists to assist with the project, legal counsel restructures the Master Services Agreements (MSAs) and Statements of Work (SOWs) to comply with subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the Act. Any Canadian arm's-length subcontractor performing eligible support work on Apex's behalf operates under a segregated SOW that explicitly specifies the technological uncertainties being investigated, confirms that the work is performed on behalf of Apex under Apex's technical direction, and vests all resulting intellectual property and technological risk exclusively in Apex. Internally, salaried employees maintain weekly contemporaneous time-sheets allocating hours strictly between eligible experimental kernel development and excluded third-party ERP connector configuration or commercial user interface development.
Case Study 2: HealthTech & Industrial IoT — Incorporating Third-Party Commercial Software into an Edge Diagnostic System
Baseline Project Scenario and the "2037625 Ontario Inc." Pitfall

An Ottawa-based medical device and software CCPC, MedStream Diagnostics Inc. (MedStream), is developing an automated point-of-care cellular diagnostic appliance. To accelerate commercial deployment, MedStream licenses a third-party commercial optical character recognition (OCR) and image-segmentation software library and incorporates this purchased software into its broader diagnostic software application running on low-power embedded edge processors. In its initial SR&ED preparation, MedStream claims all software engineering salaries and third-party contractor invoices incurred to integrate the commercial image-processing library with its proprietary patient-record software and hardware sensors. The CRA challenges the claim on audit, relying on 2037625 Ontario Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 269, to assert that incorporating purchased third-party commercial software into a larger application using the vendor's Software Development Kit (SDK) represents standard systems integration, and contrasting MedStream's sparse documentation with the successful evidentiary showing in ACSIS EHR (Electronic Health Record) Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 263.
Step 1: Technical Reframing from "Library Integration" to "Architectural & Algorithmic Modification"

To overcome the 2037625 Ontario Inc. barrier regarding third-party commercial software, MedStream must demonstrate that it did not merely use or interface the purchased software via standard procedures, but encountered a fundamental technological limitation in the underlying technology when incorporating the module into the target computational environment. MedStream's lead systems architect documents why the third-party commercial image library, when compiled and executed via standard SDK procedures on MedStream's fanless ARM-based edge microcontroller, exceeds thermal design power envelopes and suffers catastrophic floating-point quantization drift on low-contrast microfluidic cellular images.

Rather than claiming the routine SDK integration, MedStream defines the core technological uncertainty under paragraph 248(1)(c) as whether a novel hybrid fixed-point quantization wrapper and custom Direct Memory Access (DMA) pipeline can intercept and transform raw sensor tensors prior to invocation of the compiled third-party commercial binary, thereby reducing computational complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n) without degrading cellular boundary detection sensitivity below the clinical 99.4% threshold. Directly echoing the Court's cancer-cell analogy in Paragraph 35 of 2037625 Ontario Inc., MedStream proves it is not merely "looking into a microscope" via standard software tools, but is pursuing "the amalgam of two different techniques to create something new" at the algorithmic and hardware-abstraction layer—and, consistent with Paragraph 38 of the decision, must also show that the combined technique is a new technique never previously used in that particular industry.
Step 2: Implementing a Rigorous Scientific Method Protocol

MedStream establishes a structured four-stage experimental workflow aligned with the Northwest Hydraulic mandate. In the baseline verification stage, the engineering team formally documents all standard optimization techniques attempted and exhausted—including standard compiler flags, vendor-recommended thread-pooling, and image down-sampling—demonstrating quantitatively why standard practice failed to resolve the accuracy-versus-thermal trade-off. In the hypothesis design stage, the team mathematically formulates three competing algorithmic approaches to pre-filter and quantize the tensor streams before feeding the commercial software module. During the experimental prototyping stage, the engineers construct a minimal, non-commercial test harness—eligible as commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d)—solely to inject noisy microfluidic datasets and measure CPU cycle counts, thermal dissipation, and false-negative rates. Finally, in the analytical conclusion stage, the team performs a comparative statistical evaluation of the experimental runs, documenting the specific technological advancement achieved in embedded signal-processing architecture.
Step 3: Evidentiary Fortification for CRA Technical Review and Tax Court Readiness

Recognizing that the Tax Court judge evaluates the concrete evidence placed before the Court and that the Tax Court of Canada Rules require comprehensive documentary disclosure, MedStream compiles a contemporaneous "SR&ED Trial Binder" throughout the taxation year. Every experimental build is recorded in a dated technical matrix detailing the hypothesis reference, the modified algorithmic parameter, input dataset characteristics, observed quantitative output, deviation from expected results, and the subsequent experimental modification. Unlike standard commercial workflows that delete unsuccessful code branches, MedStream preserves all failed experimental Git branches and failed simulation outputs as primary physical evidence that technological risk and uncertainty were genuinely encountered and systematically investigated.
Step 4: Statutory Cost Segregation and Contract Structuring

To protect the financial integrity of the claim under section 37 and section 127 of the Act before the CRA financial reviewer concludes the audit, MedStream enforces strict accounting segregation. MedStream's tax advisor excludes the licensing cost of the third-party commercial software from the SR&ED expenditure pool, recognizing that commercial software licences are neither consumed nor transformed materials and that capital expenditures, restored to SR&ED eligibility for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, qualify only where incurred for premises, facilities or equipment used in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Furthermore, in strict compliance with CRA policy and Tax Court jurisprudence, only the rudimentary diagnostic user interface required strictly to execute the experimental tests is included under paragraph 248(1)(d), whereas all commercial graphical user interface workflows designed for clinical end-users are isolated in non-SR&ED cost centres.

Restructured Compliant Claim (Satisfying Subsection 248(1) & Northwest Hydraulic)

cells: Problem Definition (Form T661, Line 242)
Describes business and functional goals: interfacing proprietary software with third-party commercial software.
Defines system-level technological constraints where standard procedures and vendor SDKs demonstrably fail.
Methodological Approach (Form T661, Line 244)
Relies on well-known coding standards, API documentation, and routine trial-and-error debugging ("looking into a microscope").
Formulates explicit causal hypotheses, designs controlled experimental protocols, and modifies underlying algorithms and architectures.
Knowledge Advancement (Form T661, Line 246)
Claims the new interfaced software product or commercial feature as the advancement.
Articulates the specific increase in computer science or engineering knowledge resulting from resolving the architectural bottleneck.
Contemporaneous Evidence
High-level project summaries, invoices, and commercial release notes reconstructed after year-end.
Time-stamped baseline failure tests, preserved failed Git branches, quantitative benchmark logs, and hypothesis-linked tickets.
Financial & Contractual Allocation
Bundles commercial UI, COTS licensing, and broad contractor invoices into an undifferentiated claim pool.
Segregates paragraph 248(1)(d) support coding via granular time tracking; structures subcontractor SOWs strictly for SR&ED performed on the taxpayer's behalf.

body.text: Section 5: Conclusions and Strategic Imperatives for Canadian SR&ED Claimants

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in 2037625 Ontario Inc. (formerly ITC Invoice to Cash Inc.) v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 269, stands as an instructive cautionary illustration for Canadian software developers, financial technology enterprises, and systems integrators claiming SR&ED tax incentives, although, because the appeal proceeded under the Informal Procedure, section 18.28 of the Tax Court of Canada Act provides that the judgment is not to be treated as a precedent for any other case. While Canadian courts have generally recognized that the SR&ED provisions of the Income Tax Act serve the purpose of encouraging scientific research in Canada, the Court in 2037625 Ontario Inc. did not discuss purposive interpretation; the decision illustrates that a claimant must still prove, on a balance of probabilities, genuine scientific or technological uncertainty under paragraph 248(1)(c) that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures (2015 TCC 269, paras. 20–21).

Three enduring legal imperatives govern Canadian tax practitioners and technical advisors in the wake of this ruling. First, standard techniques negate technological uncertainty regardless of commercial outcome: as encapsulated in Paragraph 35 of the judgment, creating a novel, commercially valuable product or achieving functional interoperability between proprietary and third-party commercial software cannot qualify as SR&ED if the result is achieved using standard, well-known techniques. Where standard practice suffices, technological risk and uncertainty are legally non-existent. Second, baseline exhaustion must be proven contemporaneously: before claiming software interfacing or third-party module integration, claimants must establish through objective, dated benchmark evidence exactly why standard engineering procedures, public literature, and vendor SDKs were structurally incapable of achieving the required technical parameters. Finally, claimants must execute surgical segregation of project scope and expenditures, separating excluded commercial software development—such as routine API wiring, commercial user interfaces, and COTS configuration—from the underlying experimental kernel where genuine algorithmic or architectural hypotheses are systematically tested. By embedding the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria directly into engineering governance, contract drafting, and contemporaneous SDLC documentation, Canadian taxpayers can insulate valid experimental development claims from reassessment and prevail both at CRA review and before the Tax Court of Canada.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; court concluded the software project used standard development tools without achieving technological advancement.
